content: The volt, symbolized as V, is the SI-derived unit used to measure electric potential difference or electromotive force. It is named after Alessandro Volta, a Lombard physicist (1745–1827), who invented the voltaic pile, recognized as the first modern chemical battery. The volt is defined as the potential difference across a conductor when a current of one ampere dissipates one watt of power. In terms of SI base units, it is represented as m²·kg·s⁻³·A⁻¹. Alternatively, it can be expressed as one joule of energy per coulomb of electric charge (J/C). Since 1990, the volt has been internationally standardized for practical measurements using the Josephson effect. This involves a fixed conventional value for the Josephson constant, as determined by the 18th General Conference on Weights and Measures. In the hydraulic analogy, which is sometimes used to explain electrical circuits, voltage is compared to water pressure. It determines the speed at which electrons move through a circuit. Current, measured in amperes, is analogous to the volume of water flowing past a point per unit time (volumetric flow rate). The flow rate is influenced by the width of the pipe (analogous to electrical resistance) and the pressure difference between the pipe's inlet and outlet (analogous to potential difference or voltage). Power dissipation in this analogy corresponds to the product of flow rate and pressure, just as electrical power dissipation in a resistor equals the product of current and voltage drop across the resistor (amperes × volts = watts). The relationship between voltage and current in ohmic devices is governed by Ohm's Law. Examples of voltages in various applications include: Automotive batteries: approximately 12.4 V when idle and 14.4 V while charging (vehicle running). Household mains electricity: 240 V RMS in Australia, 230 V RMS in Europe, Asia, and Africa, 120 V RMS in North America, and 100 V RMS in Japan. Rapid transit third rails: 600 to 750 V. High-speed train overhead power lines: typically 25 kV RMS at 50 Hz, with exceptions depending on the system. High-voltage electric power transmission lines: starting at 110 kV RMS and reaching up to 1150 kV RMS (recorded as of 2005). Lightning: highly variable, often around 100 MV. Note: RMS (root mean square) voltage refers to the effective value of a sinusoidal signal. The peak voltage is √2 times greater than the RMS voltage for a sinusoidal waveform centered around zero volts. Historically, the volt originated in 1800 when Alessandro Volta developed the voltaic pile, a precursor to the modern battery, following a professional disagreement with Luigi Galvani over the galvanic response. Volta discovered that the most effective pair of dissimilar metals for generating electricity was zinc and silver. In the 1880s, the International Electrical Congress, now known as the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), officially adopted the volt as the unit of electromotive force. At that time, it was defined as the potential difference across a conductor when a current of one ampere dissipates one watt of power. Before the advent of the Josephson junction voltage standard, the volt was maintained in national laboratories using specially constructed batteries called standard cells. In the United States, the Weston cell design was used as the standard from 1905 to 1972.
